practicalQuestion: How should high-minute, low-minute, and returning athletes receive different strength, speed, and conditioning exposures during a short turnaround between competitions?

decisionContext.population: Collegiate roster with different recent competition exposures
decisionContext.phase: Seventy-two to ninety-six hours between competitions
decisionContext.outcome: Preserve readiness while addressing underexposure and continued progression by subgroup
decisionContext.constraints: One full-team field session; limited weight-room access; returning athletes remain under medical and rehabilitation plans

evidenceConfidence.rationale: No source in the pack tests different strength, speed, or conditioning doses for high-minute, low-minute, and returning athletes within a 72 to 96 hour turnaround. The evidence is observational and indirect. It comes from elite and professional male soccer, one reserve professional soccer squad, elite male Australian football, and media-based elite football return-to-play data. It describes load gaps by match minutes, the timing of near-maximal speed exposure, congestion and injury, wellness recovery after matches, and risk after early return. Where sources suggest subgroup handling, those are the authors' interpretations, not tested prescriptions.

dimensions.sourceReview: The sources are a retrospective multi-team cohort on near-maximal speed timing, a one-team descriptive load study limited to six-day weeks, a systematic review of eight observational congestion studies, a mixed-methods study combining 14 practitioner interviews with media-based injury data, and a retrospective cohort on prematch wellness. There is no controlled trial. A research newsletter in the pack (library ID 427) reprints the speed study abstract, so it is not counted as separate support.
dimensions.directness: Low. One club's day-after session split by recent minutes is described, but its outcomes are not tested. The speed study authors suggest that in 3 to 5 day turnarounds, D-2 speed exposure may only concern substitutes. This is their interpretation and was not analysed by minutes. No source addresses weight-room strength exposure.
dimensions.consistency: Partial. The sources address different parts of the question rather than the same outcome. Speed exposure, congestion risk, and return-to-play risk point toward different emphases. Training and overall injury findings across the congestion studies were equivocal.
dimensions.transferability: Limited. The populations are elite and professional male soccer (European clubs and one Australian league), a Spanish reserve squad with players around 20 years old, elite male Australian football players who played most of each match, and media-based elite European football data. No cited source studied collegiate or female athletes. The wellness study used 6 to 8 day microcycles, which are longer than this window.

bottomLine.text: The library has no study that tests different strength, speed, and conditioning doses for high-minute, low-minute, and returning athletes in a 72 to 96 hour turnaround. Indirect evidence from professional soccer supports four points. Players with more match minutes accumulated more weekly running load. Short turnarounds rarely included near-maximal speed exposure. The speed study authors suggest that in 3 to 5 day turnarounds such exposure may only concern substitutes. Congested schedules were usually linked with higher match injury incidence. For returning athletes, one study's preliminary data flagged high exposure after early return as high risk. Use these findings to frame options, not to set doses.

actions.title: Option: use recent match minutes as the first split
actions.text: In one Spanish reserve professional soccer squad, players with more match minutes accumulated more weekly load. Total distance and high metabolic load distance were higher in the 90-minute and over-60-minute groups than in the under-60-minute and 0-minute groups. High-speed running and sprint distance were higher in the 90-minute group than in the under-60-minute and 0-minute groups. Weekly high-speed and sprint load was double for 90-minute players compared with 0-minute players. That club split the day-after session. Players with under 60 minutes did a circuit, a small positional game and a small-sided game, while the others did a recovery session. The authors judged that this compensatory session did not seem to provide enough high-speed and sprint overload. The study analysed only six-day weeks and did not test any outcome. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): grouping the single field session by recent minutes is one way to address the low-minute load gap. The evidence does not test any top-up dose.

actions.title: Option: brief near-maximal speed exposure at D-2 for low-minute athletes only
actions.text: In elite soccer, near-maximal speed exposures were less common in shorter turnarounds. In 4 to 8 day turnarounds pooled, no match hamstring injuries followed exposures above 95% of maximal sprinting speed at D-2 (480 player-turnarounds). In contrast, there were 46 injuries in 11,168 player-turnarounds with no exposure. Injuries also occurred when exposure came at D-3 or earlier. The finding is observational and the confidence intervals overlapped. The authors suggest that D-2 exposures may concern the whole squad in 6 to 8 day turnarounds but only substitutes in 3 to 5 day turnarounds. In a 3-day turnaround, D-2 is the day after the previous match. They also suggest that practitioners likely consider maximal sprint work too demanding close to the previous match. If D-2 is used, they advise planning the earlier days so athletes do not reach D-2 with excessive neuromuscular fatigue. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): in this window, consider brief near-maximal speed exposure for low-minute athletes only, not high-minute starters.

actions.title: Option: limit added field volume for high-minute athletes
actions.text: A systematic review included eight studies in male professional soccer that defined congestion as matches with 4 or fewer days of recovery. Five studies found that congested schedules exposed players to higher match injury incidence. Findings on training and overall injury incidence were equivocal. Most included analyses covered whole teams and did not account for individual playing time, so the review does not show whether high-minute players carry the extra risk. It also does not test which load adjustment helps. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): high-minute athletes may need the least added field volume in this window.

actions.title: Keep returning athletes inside their clinical plan
actions.text: Media-based data from elite European football showed lower injury risk after longer rehab time when risk was expressed per calendar day, but not per unit of football exposure after return. The authors state that their quantitative results do not directly support delaying return. Supplementary analyses, which the authors call preliminary, suggest that high football exposure occurred virtually only after early return and that this was a high-risk combination. If this is replicable, the authors advise keeping match playing time to the strict minimum when an early return must be attempted. This advice concerns match time, not training sessions. Interviewed practitioners favored small-step progression with feedback loops, including after return to play. The congestion review authors suggest that recently injured players be closely monitored during congested schedules. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): treating clinicians should set any team-session exposure for returning athletes.

monitoring.label: Near-maximal speed exposure log
monitoring.text: Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): record whether and on which day each athlete ran above 95% of their own maximal sprinting speed during the turnaround. The cited study linked exposure timing, not subgroup, to match hamstring injuries. Its authors suggest that in 3 to 5 day turnarounds such exposure may only concern substitutes.

guardrails.text: The cited load study describes load gaps by match minutes in six-day weeks. It does not provide or test a compensatory dose, so this brief does not prescribe one.

limitations.text: The populations studied were elite European soccer teams, one Spanish reserve professional squad, male professional soccer clubs in Europe and Australia, elite male Australian football players who played most of each match, and media-based elite European football data. No cited source studied collegiate or female athletes.

The minutes-and-load study analysed only six-day weeks, not 72 to 96 hour turnarounds, and did not measure indoor training load. The wellness study used mostly 6 to 8 day microcycles. The speed timing study did include 3-day turnarounds.
All sources are observational or descriptive and cannot isolate the effect of training decisions. The congestion review mostly analysed whole teams without accounting for individual playing time.

claims.text: Fourteen interviewed practitioners in elite European football favored small-step progression with feedback loops based on the player's response over clear-cut jumps between rehab phases. They kept objective milestones at larger intervals, and they applied this to management after return to play. This is expert opinion, not tested data.

evidence.excerpt: Similarly, an approach to progression based on small steps with sincere feedback loops depending on the players response was favored over more clearcut transitions between rehab phases.

Importantly, this did not question the value of objective milestones at larger intervals which ensure overall structure, minimal requirements and communication. Importantly, this consideration included post-RTP player management.

assumptions: Returning athletes are taken to mean athletes returning from injury who remain under active medical and rehabilitation plans, so their exposure is set by treating clinicians.
A 72 to 96 hour turnaround is treated as matching the 3- and 4-day turnarounds in the speed timing study.
The timing of the single full-team field session within the 72 to 96 hour window was not specified, so the brief does not assume it falls at D-2.
coverageGaps: No study testing different strength, speed, and conditioning doses by recent match minutes within a 72 to 96 hour turnaround.
No evidence on weight-room strength exposure during short turnarounds. The minutes-and-load study did not measure indoor training load.
No controlled study testing whether compensatory or top-up training changes fitness, readiness, or injury outcomes for low-minute athletes.
No study testing team field-session exposure for athletes still under rehabilitation plans within a short turnaround.
No collegiate or female team-sport data on load differences by match minutes or on near-maximal speed timing.
